o: A Harshad number is divisible by its digit sum. Given x ≤ 100, return the digit sum if x is Harshad, else −1. For 18, digit sum 9 divides 18 → return 9. For 23, digit sum 5 does not divide 23 → return −1. With x ≤ 100 there are at most three digits, so extracting digits by repeated division (or string conversion) and one modulo test solves it instantly.
k: Digit sum via repeated divmod by 10; divisibility check is a single %.

a.i: Peel digits off x with % 10 and // 10, sum them, then test x % digitSum == 0. Constant time for the given bounds.
s: Compute s = sum of digits of x by repeated division.
If x % s == 0 return s, else return −1.
a.t: O(d) with d ≤ 3 digits — effectively constant.

a.i: Convert x to a string and sum the numeric values of its characters. Equally correct and arguably clearer; identical complexity.
s: Apply the divisibility test and return accordingly.
a.t: O(d) — one pass over the digits.

w: Either one-liner is fine in an interview; mention that digit extraction avoids allocation. Only edge cases are single-digit numbers (always Harshad, since x divides itself) and ensuring you return the digit sum, not x. Possible follow-up: count Harshad numbers in a range, or generalized divisibility by digit products (Moran numbers involve primality of x/digit-sum).
